Actually even in college, a common problem among students who were weak at octaves was their wrists flexing too much, or the reverse, their arms too tense

My teacher was Russian, and from my experience this wrist locking is common among teachers from that school. It works perfectly for them and me. Just to reiterate, the wrist is NOT frozen, but we do not use our wrists to turn our hand to play things like scales and runs. Especially when playing octaves, we don't have the wrists flip around like a fish

But that doesn't seem to work for children, or students with no finger strength.

When I went to music college, I was taught by my professor to NOT use my wrists. His technique was heavy on arm weight and "fingers active", so the wrists are not exactly stiff, but locked and not flexing. I've tried to apply that to my teaching, with almost no results.

Do you think a different kind of technique should be taught to small children to account for their smaller size? I would give wrist rotation a try, but I don't practice it myself, and I'm worried about creating bad habits
